A step function f is a function that can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals. That is, f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} c_i \chi_{I_i}(x), where I_i are intervals and c_i are constants.

To prove that a step function is Riemann Integrable, we need to show that the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value as the partition of the interval [a, b] is refined.

Let f be a step function defined on [a, b] and let P be a partition of [a, b] into n subintervals. Let I_i = [x_{i-1}, x_i] be the i-th subinterval.

The upper Riemann sum is defined as:

U(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} M_i (x_i - x_{i-1})

where M_i = sup_{x \in I_i} f(x) is the supremum of f on the i-th subinterval.

The lower Riemann sum is defined as:

L(P, f) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} m_i (x_i - x_{i-1})

where m_i = inf_{x \in I_i} f(x) is the infimum of f on the i-th subinterval.

Since f is a step function, we have that M_i = m_i for all i. Therefore, U(P, f) = L(P, f).

As the partition P is refined, the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same value, which is equal to the definite integral of f over [a, b]. Therefore, f is Riemann Integrable.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is bounded, i.e., there exists a constant M such that |f(x)| ≤ M for all x in [a, b]. If f is not bounded, the proof requires additional assumptions or modifications.
